title: Format Converter: review identities before writing real images
description: Reach Format Converter through Import, preview two real image mappings, write a separate destination and verify checkpoint reuse without changing the originals.
objectives: Distinguish image-format conversion from importing measurements and label masks.
Review source, target and acquisition identities before writing.
Preserve the source images, mapping CSV and field checkpoint together.
Interpret a zero-write Resume correctly without treating it as a pixel-integrity guarantee.
prerequisite: Reuse the two single-channel TIFFs prepared from real measured images in the Import Project tutorial. Each is the exact second image plane from its original array; the neutral fov01_C1.tif and fov02_C1.tif filenames no longer contain the original plate or well identities. This deliberately bounded example demonstrates two-dimensional TIFF conversion, not vendor readers, multichannel acquisition, Z projection or time series. There is no separate example-download, Plot, Live preview or AI control in Format Converter.

scenes.narration: Open Import from Home's Data category, then choose Format Converter in its nested tools. This converts image formats and filenames. Import Project handles the different task of bringing images, label masks and measurement tables together; do not mix the parent screen's controls with the converter inside it.

The Format Converter tab has its own Source, Destination, Preview and Convert controls. Its preview is a source-to-target table, not a live microscopy image or segmentation preview. The parent Import destination and Import button below the tab belong to the other workflow.

Choose a source folder, not an individual image. This example reuses the two real single-channel TIFFs from the Import lesson. Their pixels come from measured microscopy images, but the neutral field names are demonstration names, not the original acquisition coordinates.

Choose a new, empty destination folder separate from the source. Keep the original images and their provenance unchanged. Conversion creates new TIFFs and a mapping file; it does not reconstruct experimental metadata that was removed when these demonstration files were named.

Set Layout to images directly in source, because both files sit in one folder. Use indexed plate names and leave Resume off for this first run. For a real plate-and-well directory tree, select the matching layout and check the resulting assignments rather than copying this flat-folder choice.

Keep every Z plane. Max projection and first-plane-only options deliberately discard Z information; neither is demonstrated here. These inputs each contain one two-dimensional channel, so this recording does not establish how a particular vendor file, time series or multichannel acquisition will be interpreted.

Press the converter's Preview button. The actual plan lists two outputs from two source files, and the destination remains empty. Inspect the complete source-to-target mapping before Convert; a finished preview is not evidence that its well and channel assignments match your experiment.

Here the generated names use plate one, well A zero one, fields one and two, and channel one. Those are assigned demonstration identities. The source images originally came from different acquired wells, so this mapping must not be presented as recovered plate metadata or used to combine their treatments.

Check the From field and From channel columns alongside the generated names. The TIFF's only plane has array index zero, although its preserved pixels were extracted from channel index one in the original seven-plane array. The output filename's channel one is one-based; these three numbering contexts are not interchangeable.

The preview table is read-only. If identities are wrong, fix the source layout or conversion settings and preview again; there are no per-row edits or separate series and time selectors in this screen. Keep the original metadata available when reviewing automatic assignments.

Press Convert and read its summary. This actual run writes two new TIFFs with no failed or skipped mappings. We independently compare every output pixel, shape and data type with its source, and verify the source, field and channel identities in the mapping file. The originals remain unchanged.

Keep conversion underscore map dot C S V with the converted images and the original acquisition manifest. The map preserves source and target paths, assigned identities, source-channel metadata and conversion status. A separate run-status file records the operation, and a hidden field checkpoint supports later Resume.

Enable Resume and press Convert again with the same source, plan and destination. The application checks the compatible field checkpoint and readable TIFF metadata before reusing completed fields. It does not compare every pixel with the original source; do not describe Resume as a complete corruption audit.

The second run says zero files converted and two targets already existed. That is expected here: both planned outputs are present and unchanged. The table still displays the preview's planned status, so read the operation summary and mapping file for the actual result, not that table column alone.

Scroll the summary to see that two completed fields were resumed. The latest run-ledger entry reports empty because no source needed conversion; the first complete entry remains preserved. We accept this specific zero-write result only after verifying both reused outputs and their exact identities independently.

In Python, spacr.convert.scan reads source descriptions, plan builds the reviewed mappings, and convert writes the outputs. convert_folder is the settings-dictionary entry point. Keep conversion separate from segmentation and measurement, and validate your own acquisition dimensions before passing its images to Mask or Measure.
